newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's pension fund delay surprises managers.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's pension fund delay surprises managers.

text.p: The Mexican government's decision earlier this week to delay the privatization of the nation's pension fund system caught local fund managers by surprise and may spur adjustments in investment plans.

"We are in the process of evaluating the plan and what effect it will have on our operations," said Octavio Aguilar Valenzuela, vice-president of relations at Spain's Santander. Santander plans to form a pension fund firm with Mexican partner Grupo Financiero Invermexico.

Even though the government announced a six-month delay in dispersing government-held funds into private hands, several private companies managing pension and retirement funds, known as Afores, intend to sit tight and wait.

"We do not see elements that will truly affect our initial strategy, save the financial effect of the delay in funds we expect to generate," said Juan Manuel Villanueva, commercial director of the Afore formed by Grupo Financiero Serfin, Citibank de Mexico and Chilean AFP Habitat.

The government said it was delaying the move because of the need to overhaul codes assigned to pension fund holders. Four times more codes are registered with the National Savings Commission (Consar) than the nation's 10 million pension fund holders .
Private observers, however, suggest the government wanted to improve its 1997 budget outlook by holding on to the 30 billion pesos currently in pension funds.

Still, some pension fund managers are not complaining. In fact, Aguilar and Villanueva said an extra six months will give their companies extra time to prepare for expected stiff competition for Mexican savings.
"The competitive advantage we have is that we haven't begun publicity nor spent money on other prohibited activities," Villanueva said.
Santander will use the additional time to arrange its new alliance with Grupo Invermexico, Aguilar said.
The Mexican financial group's affiliate Banco Mexicano managed only two percent of existing pension funds as of July, compared with 4.7 percent managed by former Santander Afore associate Inverlat.
Companies have until Friday to apply with the Consar to operate Mexican pension funds
